absent: Values and layouts for EXECMEM type identifiers, cache flag, pending-free mask, free delay, huge-page size and vmalloc flags referenced by cache paths.
Structure layouts for executable cache, range, info and default info objects and vm area fields beyond the referenced members.
Implementations of range-aware vmalloc, trapping-fill, rox restore, direct-map validity, read-only-executable promotion and the primary force-writable variant.
Cache cleaning work handler, tree initialization, and shrink or teardown paths for free and busy areas.
Internal leak helpers for lookup, reference acquisition, creation, object dumping, reference release and stack-depot interaction.
Scan thread main loop, gray-list handling, automatic scan scheduling and reporting thresholds beyond colour and aging predicates.
Fault-injection framework behaviour for attribute parsing, failure decision and debugfs attribute creation.
Concurrency rules for page and slab fault-injection tunables.
Exact log formats, error codes and build conditions for executable rox support and verbose leak detection.

findings.text: Executable memory allocator selects the range for the requested type, rounds the size up to page granularity, uses the read-only-executable cache when the range is flagged for caching and otherwise allocates directly through the range-aware vmalloc path with reset-on-free semantics, then clears sanitizer tagging on the returned pointer.

Read-write executable allocator obtains memory through the main executable allocator and then transitions the whole rounded allocation to writable; failure of either allocation or permission transition yields a null result while success transfers ownership without triggering automatic release.

Executable memory release first attempts cache reclaim and only falls back to generic vmalloc release when the pointer is not owned by the cache; callers must avoid interrupt context because read-only teardown is not supported there.

Read-only-executable status query reports whether the range for a given executable memory type carries the cache flag, allowing callers to distinguish cached read-only-executable types from directly allocated types.

Page allocation fault injector decides whether a page allocation of a given order and flags should fail, applying minimum-order and flag-based exclusions before delegating to the generic fault framework with size proportional to order and with quiet handling when the caller suppresses warnings.

Architecture hook for executable memory configuration is weak and defaults to absent, signalling the generic initializer to install a vmalloc-spanning fallback range; architectures override it to supply tailored ranges.

Insertion of a freed interval into the free tree merges with touching neighbours, extending the lower bound when a predecessor ends immediately before the new block and extending the upper bound when a successor starts immediately after, then stores the coalesced extent as a single entry.

Cache candidate validation accepts an address when its whole extent lies strictly inside either the primary range or, when configured, the fallback range, so fallback provides an alternate accepted span rather than enlarging the primary.

Locked cache allocation scans free extents for the first entry that is both large enough and range-accepted, records the leading portion in the busy tree, removes the consumed extent from the free tree, reinserts any trailing remainder, and on remainder-insert failure rolls back the busy entry and reports absence.

Cache refill rounds the request up to huge-page granularity for a first vmalloc attempt with huge-mapping allowance, retries with the exact size on failure, aborts when no memory is obtained or no vm area is found, pre-fills trapping instructions, promotes to read-only-executable, and under one mutex hold adds the block and carves the request; add failure restores the direct map before freeing.
Cached allocation first attempts a mutex-guarded lookup in existing free extents and only on miss performs refill-and-carve, so steady-state hits avoid vmalloc and permission work.

Deferred-free state is encoded as a tag bit inside the busy-tree stored pointer, with dedicated helpers to test, set and clear the bit without altering the underlying address, allowing the tree to retain ownership while marking reclaim as pending.

Reclaim of a busy extent transitions it to writable, refills trapping instructions, restores read-only-executable protection, returns the extent to the free tree and removes the busy entry; any failure before the free-tree insertion aborts without mutating tree ownership.
In the fallback configuration the force-writable helper unconditionally reports success without changing protections, so read-write acquisition after allocation always succeeds in that build.
When the cache is compiled out, allocation always reports absence and release always reports not-owned, forcing all executable memory through the direct vmalloc path.

Configuration validation requires the default range to carry non-zero alignment, bounds and protection, rejects the whole configuration otherwise with a critical log, and when read-only-executable support is unavailable warns once and strips the cache flag from every configured type.

Missing per-type ranges inherit alignment, bounds, flags and fallback span from the default range, with module data forced to standard kernel protection while other empty types inherit the default protection.

Generic initialization uses architecture-supplied ranges when present, otherwise installs a default range spanning the vmalloc area with executable protection and unit alignment, then validates, fills gaps and publishes the resulting table globally.

Page fault injection never triggers below the configured minimum order, never triggers for no-fail allocations, and by default also exempts high-memory and direct-reclaim allocations, with each exemption individually tunable.

Slab fault-injection control starts with reclaim exemption enabled and cache filtering disabled, mirroring the page control shape but tracking slab-specific filtering rather than order and high-memory concerns.

Leak-scan colour derives from reference counts against a per-object minimum: white means below minimum and not blackened, gray means at or above minimum with a non-blackened minimum, with zero and minus one serving as gray and black sentinels.
An object counts as unreferenced only when it is white, still marked allocated, and its creation time plus the minimum age is at or before the last scan time, combining colour, liveness and aging.

Object hex reporting refuses physical objects, resolves per-CPU pointers through the current CPU view, truncates output to two rows, labels per-CPU dumps with length and CPU, and suspends sanitizer tracking across the dump.

Diagnostic output transparently targets either a sequence file or the warning log, with formatted messages and hex dumps each having a dual-sink helper that selects sequence output when a file is supplied and warning output otherwise, using a fixed four-space prefix for hex.

Lookup and creation helpers are thin delegations that fix hidden kind and alias arguments: exact lookups use no alias, reference-acquiring lookup mirrors plain lookup with acquisition, and creation distinguishes normal from per-CPU by a single flag while sharing size, minimum and allocation context.

Checksum reset forces the checksum to all-ones and excess-reference update stores a caller-supplied surplus count, each under the object lock with reference acquisition, warning and doing nothing when the address has no tracked object.

Scan-area registration allows alias matches, allocates a descriptor with nested allocation context, marks the whole object for full scan with a one-time warning when allocation fails, interprets maximal size as extending to the object end, rejects overruns with a warning plus diagnostic dump, and otherwise prepends the validated subrange to the object area list under lock.

Unreferenced-object reports state type-qualified pointer and size, command name with process identifier and creation time, optional hex dump, and a checksum-qualified backtrace with one symbol per frame, with the public printer always including the hex section.

Leak tracking preallocates a fixed object pool sized by configuration, maintains three initially empty red-black indexes separating normal, physical and per-CPU objects, and uses dedicated slab caches for object records and scan-area descriptors.

Global scan state tracks minimum and maximum observed addresses for normal and per-CPU memory starting from inverted extremes, a scan thread handle, minimum age and wait intervals, last-scan time, suspect count, and toggles for stack scanning, disable skipping and leak-found indication.

The executable cache mutex serializes all free-tree and busy-tree mutations, including coalescing insertion, first-fit carving, refill add-plus-carve atomicity, immediate reclaim and deferred-tag updates, with both scoped guards and explicit hold-across-refill used to keep add and consume atomic.

Each tracked leak object carries its own raw spinlock held with interrupt state saved across checksum, excess-reference, flag and scan-area list mutations, always paired with reference acquisition before locking and release after unlocking.
A dedicated scan mutex exists to serialize leak-scan activity against concurrent tracking updates, separate from per-object locks and the executable cache mutex.

Leak object record combines synchronization and linkage with lifetime and diagnostics: lock plus status and deletion state, global and gray list links with red-black and reclaim hooks, reference counting, pointer with size and surplus reference, minimum and observed counts with unreferenced-scan tally, integrity checksum with stack handle, scan-area list head, creation time with process identity and command name, and a scan-local duplicate tally.

Scan-area descriptor links into its owning object and delimits a subrange to examine, holding list linkage with start address and byte length, where an empty list on the owner implies whole-object scanning.

Page fault-injection control block groups a generic fault attribute with two boolean exemptions for high-memory and reclaim allocations and a minimum order threshold, defaulting to exemptions enabled and threshold of one.
Slab fault-injection control block groups a generic fault attribute with a reclaim exemption and a cache-filter toggle, defaulting to exemption enabled and filtering disabled.

Cached executable extents move between free and busy with a deferred path: busy entries whose immediate reclaim fails are tag-marked and counted with delayed retry scheduled; a background handler clears tags and retries, rescheduling delay while any remain and otherwise scheduling cleanup, while successful immediate reclaim schedules cleanup directly.

Leak candidates progress by colour and aging: counts below minimum stay white, counts reaching minimum become gray unless blackened, and only white allocated objects older than the minimum age at last scan are reported, with checksum and reference updates influencing later scans.

Executable memory initialization progresses from architecture setup through validation and gap filling to publication, aborting publication on validation failure and otherwise installing either tailored or fallback ranges before any allocation is served.
Early and late initializers both invoke the common executable memory setup, providing two boot-time entry hooks that converge on the same validation and publication sequence.

Page fault injection exposes a boot-parameter hook that forwards its string to the generic fault-attribute parser and a debug filesystem initializer that publishes the fault attribute plus toggles for reclaim and high-memory exemption and an integer for minimum order.

Slab fault injection exposes a boot-parameter hook forwarding to the generic fault parser and a debug filesystem initializer publishing the fault attribute with reclaim-exemption and cache-filter toggles, failing cleanly when attribute creation reports an error.

Deferred-free background handler acts as a workqueue entry that exits immediately when no pending count remains and otherwise sweeps busy entries for tagged pointers, attempting reclaim and maintaining the pending count and follow-up scheduling.
Freeing executable memory from interrupt context triggers a warning because read-only vmalloc teardown is not interrupt-safe, so callers must defer release to process context.

Refill without holding the cache mutex across block insertion and request carving would allow a concurrent allocator to consume the fresh block, which is why the implementation requires atomic add-plus-allocate.

Allocation and reclaim paths handle resource exhaustion without leaking ownership: remainder-insert failure rolls back the busy entry, reclaim-allocation failure defers via tag and delayed work rather than dropping the busy entry, and refill-add failure restores the direct map before freeing.

Leak diagnostics avoid false or unsafe output by refusing hex dumps of physical objects, forcing full-object scans when scan-area allocation fails, and rejecting oversized scan ranges with a warning and object dump instead of recording them.

Leak scan sizing and timing facts: stack depth sixteen, minimum reporting age five thousand milliseconds, first scan after sixty seconds, subsequent scans spaced six hundred seconds, largest scanned block four thousand ninety-six bytes, pointer stride equal to native pointer size.
Scan colour sentinel values are zero denoting gray and minus one denoting black.
Object status flag positions occupy distinct low bits: allocated bit zero, reported bit one, no-scan bit two, full-scan bit three, physical bit four, per-CPU bit five, suspect bit six.
Deletion-state flags use bit zero for removed and bit one for no-delete.
Hex dump formatting facts: line prefix of four spaces, row length sixteen bytes, grouping of one, ASCII rendering enabled, at most two lines per object.

Default leak-detector tunables: tracking and free tracking enabled, stack scanning enabled, minimum unreferenced scans two in verbose builds and one otherwise, with late-initialized, error, last-scan, wait, suspect, skip-disable and leak-found state starting cleared.
